opening_summary: Thirty-four terms for how things move in a game, from keys and easing to poses, rigs and state machines. The exact term lets you ask an AI coding agent for the motion you mean.
opening_description: 34 animation terms: keys, easing, craft, rigs.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often think an animation stores every frame of a move. It does not. A keyframe stores one value at one time, and the engine computes every frame in between. Animation is full of look-alike pairs like that one. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
A keyframe stores
every frame of the move.

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-four terms in four groups, each about how a value or a body changes over time. The first group is keys and in-betweens. Keyframe, interpolation, clip, tween, linear, step and cubic. What an animation stores, and how the gaps get filled.

The second group is easing and time. Easing, ease-in, ease-out, timing and spacing, frame rate, playback speed scale, loop, loop seam and cycle. These say how motion speeds up, slows down and repeats.
The third group is the craft. Pose, silhouette, weight and balance, anticipation, squash and stretch, arcs, follow-through and secondary motion. These are what make motion read as alive.

The fourth group is bodies and control. Rig and skeleton, rest pose, skinning weights, FK and IK, forward and inverse kinematics, then retargeting, root motion, in-place, blend tree and state machine. These say how a body is built, posed and driven.

A plot of one value, position x, against time. A Keyframe is a value you store at a specific time. In this made-up example there are three, twenty at zero seconds, eighty at one second and fifty at two. Nothing is stored between them. For example, the sword's fast attack in Walker's finite state machine build stores a few rotation keys, the blade's angle at the start, at the top of the swing, and where it settles.

Interpolation is computing the values between the keys. Its results are the in-betweens, the open dots on the line. Only three keys are stored, and every other value is worked out when it is needed. At half a second it gives fifty. For example, between the sword's few stored angles, Godot computes the blade's angle on every frame of the swing, so nobody has to key each frame by hand.

Now three small plots, one each for x, rotation and scale. A Clip is an authored animation, a bundle of tracks, each track holding its own keys over time. Someone makes it ahead of time and saves it. For example, the sword's fast attack in Walker is one clip, saved in the sword scene, with a track for the blade's rotation and a track of calls that open the window for the next swing of the combo.

A Tween is interpolation driven by code. It stores no keys. Code gives a start, an end and a duration, here x from zero to one hundred over one and a half seconds. The clip stored nine keys, and the tween stores none. For example, a health bar that glides to whatever the player's health is right now is a tween, because its end value comes from play, not from a file.

A plot of the same four keys, with ways to join them. Linear means a constant rate of change from one key to the next, a straight line with a sharp corner at each key. At three seconds it reaches one hundred. For example, a moving platform keyed with linear between two ledges travels at one steady speed and turns around at each end without slowing down.

The dashed staircase is Step, also called discrete. The value holds at one key until the next key, then jumps, with nothing in between. For example, a key that switches a sword's hitbox on or off should be step, because there is no value halfway between on and off. The hitbox is either live or it is not.

The red curve is Cubic, a smooth curve through the keys, with no corner at any key. The price is that it can overshoot. Here it bends past seventy and past one hundred before it turns back. The drawing shows the idea, not Godot's exact formula. For example, a floating gem keyed to bob through four heights moves smoothly with cubic, but may rise a little above its highest key.

A curve of progress against time, and two columns of dots showing where an object is at equal time steps. Easing is the speed curve of a change, how fast it goes at each moment of the move. Ease-in-out, drawn here, is slow at both ends. Its speed is zero, then one point five in the middle, then zero. For example, a pause menu panel that starts gently, speeds up and settles softly into place is eased.

The curve now starts flat. Ease-in means a slow start that then speeds up, so the first steps are tiny and the last ones are big. Its speed rises from zero to two. For example, a heavy stone door in a dungeon level that creaks open slowly, then swings faster and faster, is ease-in.

Now the curve ends flat. Ease-out is the opposite, a fast start that slows to a stop, so the move brakes into its end. The red dots bunch at the top, where it finishes. For example, a camera that sweeps quickly toward the player and then settles gently onto them uses ease-out.

Two bars, the same move made twice. Timing and spacing is one entry with two halves. Timing is how long a move takes. Spacing is how far it moves from one frame to the next. Here only the timing changes. At sixty frames per second, half a second is thirty frames and one and a half seconds is ninety. For example, if an enemy's sword swing is retimed to take half as many frames, it lands sooner and the player has less time to react.

Now the spacing. Both rows have the same twelve frames, so the timing is the same. In the top row every gap is equal, and the motion looks constant. In the bottom row the gaps start small, grow toward the middle and shrink again, so it looks eased. Close dots read as slow, far dots as fast. For example, a door in your level that opens in the same number of frames can feel heavy or light from its spacing alone.

Three rows, the same one second of motion sampled three ways. Frame rate is how many frames are shown per second. At twelve frames per second the dot jumps up to one hundred nine pixels between pictures, and at sixty only twenty-two. For example, when the Walker sword test runs from the command line it fixes the frame rate, so every frame is the same slice of game time and a key lands on the same frame in every run.

Three bars for one clip that lasts two seconds. Playback speed scale is a multiplier on how fast a clip plays. At two, the clip ends in one second. At one half, it takes four. The keys themselves do not change. For example, the Walker three D platformer plays the robot's running blend through a time scale node, so its idle, walk and run clips play faster than they were keyed, and nobody edits a key.

A plot of hip height, one clip of one second played three times. A Loop is a clip that starts again from its first frame when it ends. The clock keeps running, but the clip time wraps, so at three seconds the clip is back at zero. For example, in the Walker three D platformer the robot's idle, walk and run clips are set to loop, while its shooting clips play once and stop.

Two clips of the same length with two different endings. A Loop seam is a visible jump where the last frame meets the first. In the red clip the last key is not the first, so every wrap jumps forty pixels. In the black clip they match, and the jump is zero. For example, a sprite sheet walk whose last frame does not match its first makes the character hitch once every stride.

Two leg angles across one stride, and a stick figure walking. A Cycle, for a walk or a run, is one full stride that repeats, with the first and last poses matching. The red leg is the black leg shifted by half a cycle. In this example each leg swings to thirty-two degrees. For example, the walk on your character's sprite sheet is a cycle, a few frames for one step with each foot, played over and over while the player moves.

Three stick figures with their feet on the ground. A Pose is a single held body position, and animation is a series of them. These three poses, standing, crouching and reaching up, are three keys, and the engine or the animator fills in the rest. A pose is a body position, and a keyframe is any stored value. For example, Clawd in Walker shows one fixed jump pose for the whole time it is in the air.

The same action drawn twice, as solid shapes. A Silhouette is the solid outline of a pose, and a clear action reads from the outline alone. With the arms out the shape is two hundred twenty-eight pixels wide and says what is happening. With the arms in front it is thirty-eight, and says nothing. For example, a knight holding a sword out to the side reads as armed even when tiny on screen, while a sword held flat against the body disappears into the outline.

A leaning figure, with a dot for its centre of gravity and a bar for its feet. Weight and balance is where the balance falls. A pose is stable while the centre of gravity sits over the feet. Past the feet, the body must fall or take a step. Here the dot ends inside the feet, so it is balanced. For example, a character leaning over a ledge to look down needs a planted foot under its weight, or it looks about to topple.

A red ball on the ground. Anticipation is a short wind-up that tells the player an action is coming. Here the ball squashes down for zero point three five seconds, twenty-one frames at sixty frames per second, before it leaves the ground. For example, an enemy that pulls its arm back before it throws a rock gives the player a moment to see the attack coming and dodge.

Now two hops. Squash and stretch means the shape changes with the motion. It compresses on impact and elongates at speed, which shows how springy the thing is and how it carries its speed. Here it stretches up to one point three in flight and squashes to zero point six two on landing, while width times height stays at one. For example, a slime enemy in a platformer flattens wide when it lands and stretches tall as it springs up.

One hop, drawn as a path. Arcs means that limbs and thrown things move along curves, not straight lines. Without gravity the ball would follow the grey straight line. With gravity the path bends. The dots are twelve frames at equal times, so they crowd at the top. For example, a grenade the player lobs should travel in a curve, and so should the tip of a sword as it swings around the shoulder.

A block that moves and stops, with a red tail behind it. Follow-through means parts keep moving after the body stops, each settling in its own time. In this simulated run the body stops at four hundred fifty, and the tail swings one hundred three pixels past its rest place before it settles. For example, the Walker sword's fast attack swings the blade past the angle where it ends, then settles it back, so the swing does not stop dead.

Three bars, for the shoulder, the elbow and the hand. This is overlap, the other half of that entry. Parts start and stop at different times. In this simulated run each part makes the same move zero point one two seconds after the one before, so the hand stops zero point two four seconds after the shoulder. For example, when your character throws a punch, the shoulder leads, the elbow follows and the fist arrives last, which keeps the move from looking stiff.

A head that moves side to side, with a strand of hair. Secondary motion is extra movement the main action causes, such as a tail or hair, that nobody keys by hand. The head is keyed. The hair's six points are computed on each of two hundred forty frames, one thousand four hundred forty positions. For example, you can ask an AI coding agent for a short script that makes a character's ponytail trail after its head, so only the head needs keys.

Two bones joined at an elbow. Rig and skeleton go together. The skeleton is a hierarchy of bones, and the rig is that skeleton plus the binding that makes the mesh follow it. Turn the upper arm and the forearm follows, here bending to eighty degrees. For example, the robot model in the Walker three D platformer brings its own skeleton inside its model file, and its mesh moves when the animation turns those bones.

Now a mesh is bound to the bones. The Rest pose, also called the bind pose, is the skeleton's default pose, the one the mesh was fitted to. Here every angle is zero and the arm is straight. Bend the elbow with each point tied to only one bone, and the mesh splits at the joint. For example, a character modelled in Blender standing straight with arms out is bound in that pose, and you can return the skeleton to it at any time.

The same mesh, shaded by how much each point follows the forearm. Skinning weights, also called bone weights or vertex weights, say how strongly each vertex follows each bone. Near the elbow the weights blend, so the point at the elbow follows each bone by one half and the bend stays smooth. For example, in Godot you paint the weights on a two D character's polygon, white for full weight and black for none, so its knee bends without a gap.

A two-bone arm, swinging from the shoulder. Forward kinematics, FK, means you rotate the joints from parent to child, shoulder first, then elbow, and the hand lands wherever those angles put it. Here the elbow stays at forty degrees while the shoulder sweeps, so the hand traces an arc. Angles go in, and the hand comes out. For example, posing a wave in Blender by turning the shoulder, then the elbow, then the wrist is FK.

Now a target moves and the arm follows it. Inverse kinematics, IK, works the other way. You give a target, and the solver works out the joint angles. Once the target passes the reach limit, three hundred seventy pixels, the arm goes straight and misses. For example, in one scene of Walker's three D IK build, moving the mouse moves a target in front of the camera, and an IK node on each arm pulls the robot's arms toward it.

One clip on two skeletons. Retargeting is applying an animation made for one skeleton to a different one. The grey arm copies the angles, and on its different bone lengths the hand misses the target by seventy-one pixels. The red arm is retargeted with IK for the new skeleton, and it lands. For example, a run captured from video of one person must be retargeted onto your character's own bone names and proportions before your game can use it.

A stick figure walking along a ruler. Root motion means the clip itself moves the character through the world. The clip's root track travels, so each foot stays put on the ground. In this simulated run the root covers one hundred twenty pixels per cycle, and four hundred eighty after four seconds. For example, in a lunge or a vault the clip carries the body forward, and the code reads that motion each frame and applies it to the character.

The same walk clip, two ways to travel. In-place means the clip stays on the spot and code does the travel. If the code's speed differs from the stride, the feet skate. Here code moves the body one hundred fifty pixels a second over a stride worth one hundred twenty, so the feet skate thirty. For example, the robot in the Walker three D platformer uses no root motion. Its clips play in place, and its player script moves the body.

A speed slider over three clips, idle, walk and run. A Blend tree is a weighted mix of clips driven by parameters. One number decides how much of each clip plays. At a speed of zero point four here, the mix is zero point two idle and zero point eight walk. For example, on every physics tick the Walker three D platformer's player script writes the robot's speed into its blend tree, so the gait follows the speed with no change of state.

Three boxes, Idle, Walk and Jump, joined by arrows. A State machine has one active state at a time, and a transition fires when its condition becomes true. In this simulated run, speed rises past zero point one and Idle becomes Walk. Pressing jump sends it to Jump, and landing on the floor returns it to Walk. For example, an AI coding agent gave the Walker three D platformer's robot a state machine with three states, ground, jump and fall, driven by its physics.

Each pair puts two look-alike terms side by side. Timing is how long the move takes, half a second on top and a full second below. Spacing is where the frames fall inside it, even gaps, or gaps that grow and then shrink.
Ease-in starts slow, then speeds up, and its black curve starts flat. Ease-out starts fast, then slows to a stop, and its red curve ends flat. Slow start, or slow end.

FK takes the angles in and gives the hand position out. On the left, the shoulder and elbow angles are set. IK takes a hand target in and gives the angles out. On the right, the solver works out the elbow, forty-eight degrees.
A Blend tree says how much of each clip, here all walk and no idle. A State machine says which clip plays, and when it switches, here from Idle to Walk once the speed passes zero point one.

Each row turns a vague request into an exact instruction. Make it feel smoother becomes, ease-in-out the move of zero point four seconds between keys, so speed is zero at both ends. The chart shows the speed peaking at one point five in the middle.
Make it snappier becomes, cut the move from twelve frames to six at sixty frames per second, and use ease-out. Half the frames is half the time, zero point two seconds down to zero point one.
The walk jumps when it loops becomes, set the last key equal to the first and use the loop mode named loop linear. The jump at the seam falls from forty pixels to zero.
Make the jump feel heavier becomes, add six frames of anticipation and squash to a height of zero point seven five on landing. The ball widens to one point three three, so its area stays at one.

The hand should reach the cup becomes, use two-bone IK with the cup as the target, bones of one hundred thirty and one hundred ten, and a reach limit of two hundred forty. The cup sits at two hundred, in reach, so the solver finds the angles.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you ship an animation. First, do the key poses tell the story, and does each one read as a clear silhouette?
Second, what sits between the keys? Linear, step and cubic fill the same gaps differently, and only step holds a value and then jumps.
Third, does the easing match the weight? Heavy things want gentle starts, and most moves want a soft stop rather than a dead halt.
Fourth, do the timing and spacing still hold at the frame rate and the playback speed scale the game will really use?
Fifth, is the loop closed? The last key should equal the first, so there is no loop seam each time the clip wraps.
Sixth, who moves the body, root motion or code, and do the skinning weights bend the mesh cleanly? Then say it exactly. Not make it smoother, but ease-in-out over zero point four seconds.

recap_lines: A keyframe is a stored value, and interpolation computes the in-betweens.
Easing is the speed curve. Ease-in starts slow, and ease-out ends slow.
Timing is how long a move takes, and spacing is where its frames fall.
Anticipation is the wind-up, and squash and stretch shows speed and impact.
FK takes angles and gives the hand, and IK takes a target and gives angles.
A blend tree mixes clips by weight, and a state machine picks one clip.

your_turn.command: Give me short cases from making a game, one at a time, each showing an animation problem or choice. Draw on keyframe, tween, ease-in, ease-out, timing, spacing, loop seam, anticipation, IK and root motion. I answer with the exact term and say why its look-alike does not fit. Wait for my answer before you reveal yours, then say whether I was right.
checks: Check: each case is about making a game, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and ruled out its look-alike.

deck_problems: Slide 5 (Timing, spacing, frame rate and speed scale), step 3: the caption says 'At 12 fps the dot jumps 113 px at the start; at 60 fps it jumps 23 px', but the computed labels on the same picture say 'biggest jump 109 px' and 'biggest jump 22 px' (680 x ease-out of 1/12 is 108.6, of 1/60 is 22.5). The caption numbers are hard-coded and wrong. The narration speaks 109 and 22.

Slide 8 (Anticipation, squash and stretch, arcs), step 1: the readout ends on 'flight: 1.55 s', which is the time since the wind-up began (0.35 + 1.2), while the line above says 'then flight 1.2 s'. The readout's label should not be 'flight'. Not spoken.

Slide 9 (Follow-through, overlap, secondary motion), notes: the tail spring is described as 'omega 14, damping ratio 0.22', but the code (SPR) uses w = 9 and z = 0.2. The step 1 caption 'settles in about 1 s' also does not match the graph, where the tail is still swinging visibly past 2 s of the 4 s plot.

Slide 9 step 3: the caption says 'Keyed by hand: the head, 5 keys (diamonds)', but only three diamonds are visible, because the keys at 0 s, 1 s and 2 s are drawn at the same spot. The narration says only that the head is keyed.

Slide 3 and slide 15 call step (discrete) an interpolation ('Which interpolation sits between the keys: linear, step or cubic?'). Chapter 10 keeps two settings apart: interpolation per track (nearest, linear, cubic) and update mode per value track (UPDATE_DISCRETE). In Godot's own words the step look is nearest interpolation or the discrete update mode, so the slide's grouping can mislead a student about where the setting lives.

Slide 12 (Root motion, blend tree, state machine): step 1 gives the root track as '120 px per cycle', step 2 as '120 px/s'. They agree only if one cycle lasts one second, which the slide never states.
Slide 14 step 1: the 'eased: peak 1.5' label is drawn on the linear line, struck through by it, and well below the red peak it names.

Slide 2 step 4: 'Keys stored by the clip above: 3 tracks x 3 keys = 9' refers to a clip that is no longer on screen at that step (the tween picture has replaced it). Steps 3 and 4 also have the 'in the book text' badge of Clip sitting on its definition line, so 'tracks of values over time' runs under the badge.

Slide 10 step 1: the 'joint' label is drawn under the forearm bone, which crosses through the word. Slide 11 step 3: the grey copied-angles arm runs down over the caption 'target scaled by reach ratio'.
